clue.text: With doubly posh fellow other virtues point to modesty

parts.note: posh is used twice over: U is the crossword letter for upper-class, and a posh fellow is a nob
a nob is a toff, a posh fellow

indicators.note: other asks for the letters of virtues in a different arrangement

parts.note: a ness is a headland or point, as in Loch Ness or Sheerness

explanation.surface: A toff with all his other good qualities points the way to humility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubly' tells you posh does two jobs: the crossword letter for upper-class, then the posh fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping oneself out of sight and unassertive is a form of humility, so the noun is a synonym.

clue.text: A rebel's elevated goal, the world of learning

parts.note: Jack Cade led the Kentish rebellion of 1450

indicators.note: in a down clue, elevated means the word goal is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a goal is an aim

explanation.surface: A rebel aims high, at the world of scholarship.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack CADE was an English rebel leader of 1450; 'elevated' turns AIM upwards into MIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Academia is the collective name for universities and scholarly life, the realm of learning.

clue.text: Was candidate to be put in the ground?

definitions.meaning: to stand for election is to be a candidate, past tense
a post or plant set upright in the earth has been ... there

explanation.walkthrough: The British say a candidate stands for election rather than runs; 'to be' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are the past of stand: offering oneself for election, and setting something upright in place.

clue.text: Refusal to include pollarded tree in mock sea battle

indicators.note: to include means the refusal word wraps around the tree's letters

parts.note: nay is an old word of refusal, no

indicators.note: pollarding cuts the top off a tree, and in a down clue the top is the first letter

parts.note: the sumach is a shrub or small tree

explanation.surface: Someone declines to put a cropped tree into a staged naval fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The sumach (also spelt sumac) is a shrub; 'pollarded' lops its head and 'to include' puts what remains inside the refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: A naumachia or naumachy was a staged naval battle shown as a spectacle in ancient Rome.

clue.text: Plump for Mercury without funny hat, the old perpetual roller

parts.note: plump means fat

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the god's name wraps around the rest

parts.note: Hermes is the Greek counterpart of the Roman god Mercury

indicators.note: funny suggests the letters of hat are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone opts for the messenger god minus his comic headgear, rolling on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, wrapping the god round the 'funny' scramble. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The personified river of London is pictured as an old man who keeps rolling along, like Ol' Man River.

clue.text: Woodwork at the fish gate

parts.note: the carp is a freshwater fish
a gate is a way in, an entry

explanation.surface: Joinery done at a gate where fish are sold.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpentry is the craft of working timber, which is what woodwork means.

clue.text: A spirit favouring the young

parts.note: Geist is German for spirit or ghost, familiar from poltergeist and zeitgeist

explanation.surface: A ghost that is partial to youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ageist discriminates by age, typically against the old and so in favour of the young.

clue.text: Deserter, first following through (unnamed) in vocal work, is unacceptable

indicators.note: following signals the letter for first comes after the deserter

parts.note: per means through or by means of, as in per post

indicators.note: in means the word for unnamed goes inside the vocal work

parts.note: a song is a piece of vocal music
anon, short for anonymous, means unnamed
a rat is one who deserts a sinking cause
A is first, as in an A grade or first letter

explanation.surface: A turncoat, who first follows through on an anonymous song, is unwelcome.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(unnamed)' is printed inside the clue just as its letters sit inside the vocal work. 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A persona non grata is someone who is unwelcome or unacceptable, a Latin diplomatic term, here stood in for by its sense.

clue.text: Action in a struggle with tobacco

indicators.note: struggle suggests the words being wrestled into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'struggle' rearranges ACTION IN A; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicotiana is the botanical genus of the tobacco plant.

clue.text: Original Englishman's club is L-shaped

parts.note: the Angles were among the Germanic settlers who gave England its name
an iron is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: An early Englishman's cudgel turns out to be bent at a right angle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Angle iron is metal bar with an L-shaped cross-section; the adjective describes it rather than naming it.

clue.text: Piece of garden space, not near church, to stage shenanigans

parts.note: a flower bed is a piece of garden
room means space
far is the opposite of near
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A patch of garden, some distance from the church, becomes a setting for mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link; the answer is also the name of an Alan Ayckbourn comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedroom farce is a stage comedy of sexual intrigue and mix-ups, which is theatrical shenanigans.

clue.text: Poet and actor are like in dances

indicators.note: in means the word for like goes inside the dances

parts.note: hops are informal dances
kin, as in akin, means alike or related

explanation.surface: A poet and an actor turn out to be similar at dances.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerard Manley Hopkins was a Victorian poet and Anthony Hopkins is the actor. 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname is shared by poet Gerard Manley Hopkins and actor Sir Anthony Hopkins.

clue.text: Bump up the racket?

definitions.meaning: to ... up, or ..., is to push prices higher
British slang for a swindle or racket

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bump' also suggests a speed hump, another sense of the word, but here it is raising prices. 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramp means to raise prices sharply, and in British slang it is also a swindle or racket.

clue.text: Anticyclones grant opportunity for football club

indicators.note: an opportunity is a chance, and these letters fall by chance into a new order

explanation.surface: High-pressure weather gives a football team its chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opportunity' signals the rearrangement of ANTICYCLONES GRANT; 'for' is a link. Accrington Stanley is a Lancashire football club, famous for folding in 1962 and later returning.
explanation.definitionFit: Accrington Stanley is an English professional football club from Lancashire.

clue.text: Fry it with oil and delete rococo quality

indicators.note: rococo means elaborately ornate, so the letters are fancifully rearranged

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for delete in proofreading

explanation.surface: Cook something in oil and remove the ornate flourishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'and' are links; 'rococo' shuffles the fodder. The surface's 'rococo quality' is also what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: Floridity, ornate over-elaboration, is a quality, here coloured by the neighbouring word rococo.

clue.text: See 14
See 19
With discipline sometimes for the birds

definitions.meaning: acting ... means acting with firm discipline
the idiom ... for the birds means worthless, so the word sometimes comes before for the birds

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a fill-in-the-blank: 'strictly for the birds' is a US idiom meaning trivial or worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictly means with rigour and discipline, and it is the word in the idiom calling something fit only for birds.

clue.text: Work up during morning tea?

indicators.note: during means the reversed work goes inside the morning word

parts.note: early means in the morning

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for work is read backwards

parts.note: the erg is a unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: Getting up for work in the morning over a cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The erg is a physics unit, so 'Work' is not labour here; 'up' turns it and 'during' places it inside the morning word.
explanation.definitionFit: Earl Grey is a black tea flavoured with bergamot, named after a British prime minister.

clue.text: Change around, alien to Ireland (South), to encourage advance of professional

indicators.note: around means the change word wraps the alien and Ireland

parts.note: vary means change
ET is the alien from the Spielberg film
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland
urge means encourage
on means forward, as in to go on or advance

explanation.surface: A professional, having shifted, a foreigner to Ireland, is urged to press on southwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'to's and 'of' are links; 'around' wraps the change word round the alien and the poetic Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A veterinary surgeon is a qualified animal doctor, a member of a profession.

clue.text: See 5
Salad Days, say, soon coming up

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the pieces are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: eg (for example) means say
anon is old-fashioned for soon

explanation.surface: A musical, for instance, that's about to open.
explanation.walkthrough: Salad Days is a 1950s British musical, but here it is Shakespeare's phrase for youthful inexperience. 'coming up' reverses EG ANON as one run.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's salad days are green youth, and nonage is the period of being under age.

clue.text: See 10
See 11
Report of joints at hide-out in London

indicators.note: report of means the words are heard rather than seen

parts.note: knees are joints and a den is a hide-out

explanation.surface: News of a gang's base in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Neasden is a suburb in north-west London, long a running joke in Private Eye. 'at' only links the two words heard.
explanation.definitionFit: Neasden is a district of north-west London, so it is a place found in London.

clue.text: Horse for battery?

definitions.meaning: the device used for a battery to restore its power

explanation.walkthrough: Battery suggests artillery, which fits the warhorse sense, but the second sense is the electrical gadget.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger is both a knight's warhorse and a device that recharges batteries.

clue.text: Course of Spenser's 20

definitions.meaning: Edmund Spenser's Prothalamion repeats the refrain addressing the river in 20-down with this word

explanation.walkthrough: The refrain of Spenser's Prothalamion begins 'Sweet Thames, run softly'. 'Course' looks like the river's flow but is the dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet is the dessert course of a British meal, and Spenser's epithet for the river.

clue.text: Bird, no chicken, entering award with the others

indicators.note: entering means the not-young word goes inside the award

parts.note: GC is the George Cross, a British gallantry award
no chicken is an idiom for no longer young, so old
the rest means the others

explanation.surface: A bird past its youth gets into the honours alongside everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no chicken' is the idiom 'no spring chicken'; the GC (George Cross) is a British medal. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The goldcrest is Britain's smallest bird, a tiny kinglet with a yellow crown stripe.
